title: Demonstrate knowledge of good agricultural practices for the production of export quality perishable produce

lessons.title: Planning and orchard practices for export quality
lessons.html:
Quality starts with planning

Export quality fruit is grown, not sorted. The packhouse can only remove bad fruit; it cannot make fruit better. Good agricultural practices (GAP) start long before harvest, with decisions about where and what to plant and how the orchard is managed. Schemes such as GLOBALG.A.P. set out these practices and audit them, and most export markets and retailers require certification.

Planning decisions

  • Site and soil: choose land with suitable soil depth, drainage and climate for the crop. Do soil analysis before planting and correct pH and nutrients.
  • Cultivar and rootstock: choose cultivars that the target market wants and that suit the area. Use certified, disease-free nursery trees or vines.
  • Water: secure a reliable, legal water supply. Water use is regulated under the National Water Act 36 of 1998.
  • Market registration: register the production unit (PUC) for the intended markets early, because some markets need orchard registration and pest monitoring for a full season.

Orchard management practices

  • Nutrition: fertilise according to soil and leaf analysis. Too much nitrogen can reduce colour and storage quality; calcium matters for disorders like bitter pit in apples.
  • Irrigation scheduling: use soil moisture probes or scheduling so trees are not stressed, and avoid excess water before harvest, which can cause splitting.
  • Pruning and canopy management: let light and air into the canopy for colour, size and less disease.
  • Integrated pest management (IPM): scout for pests, use thresholds, encourage natural enemies and spray only when needed with registered products under Act 36 of 1947.
  • Soil conservation: protect soil from erosion, in line with the Conservation of Agricultural Resources Act 43 of 1983.

Records and people

Keep records of every spray, fertiliser application, irrigation and scouting result. Train workers in hygiene, safe chemical handling and quality picking. Provide toilets and hand-washing stations. Auditors will check these records and talk to workers.

lessons.title: Pre-harvest preparation and harvesting practices
lessons.html:
Pre-harvest preparations and enhancements

In the weeks before harvest, the grower takes steps to improve quality and prepare for picking:

  • Thinning: removing excess fruitlets earlier in the season gives bigger, better-quality fruit.
  • Colour enhancement: pruning or leaf removal around fruit, and reflective ground covers in some orchards, improve red colour. Any plant growth regulator must be registered and used according to the label.
  • Pre-harvest sprays: fungicide programmes protect against rots, but the pre-harvest interval on every label must be respected and the product must be accepted by the target market.
  • Residue planning: check maximum residue limits of each market and, where needed, test fruit before harvest.
  • Equipment and staff: clean bins, crates, picking bags and ladders; train pickers on maturity and handling.

Determining the harvest window

The harvest window is the period when fruit is mature enough to meet export standards and will still store and ship well. It is determined by:

  • Maturity indices for the crop: firmness, TSS, starch, ground colour for apples and pears; dry matter for avocados; juice, TSS and acid for citrus; TSS and TSS:acid for grapes.
  • Sampling fruit from representative trees in each block at regular intervals before harvest and plotting results.
  • Market and storage plans: fruit for long storage or distant markets may be picked at an earlier stage within the window than fruit for immediate sale.

Harvesting practices that protect quality

  • Pick in the cooler part of the day where possible.
  • Pick by colour or size in several rounds if the crop matures unevenly.
  • Use clippers where required (citrus) and cut stems short to avoid punctures.
  • Place, do not drop, fruit into bags and bins.
  • Do not overfill bins or crates.
  • Keep picked fruit in the shade and deliver it to the packhouse promptly.
  • Never place crates directly on soil or let animals near harvested fruit.

Every bin must be labelled with block, date and picker team so the fruit is traceable.

lessons.title: Post-harvest transport, storage and treatment
lessons.html:
Best practices after harvest

Fruit begins to lose quality the moment it is picked. Post-harvest practices aim to slow this down and to prevent damage and contamination.

Transport from orchard to packhouse

  • Use clean trailers and bakkies; do not carry chemicals, fuel or animals with fruit.
  • Drive slowly on farm roads to avoid bruising, especially with soft fruit.
  • Cover loads with shade cloth or tarpaulins to protect from sun and dust.
  • Deliver promptly; do not leave bins standing in the sun at the packhouse gate.

Receiving and storage

  • Record bins on arrival with block, date and time.
  • Move fruit quickly into a cool area or precooler.
  • Follow the cooling and storage regime for the crop and market: correct temperature, humidity and, where used, controlled atmosphere.
  • Keep storage rooms clean, and separate ethylene-sensitive products from ethylene producers.

Post-harvest treatments

  • Fungicide drenches, dips or sprays and waxes must be registered for that use, mixed at the correct concentration and monitored. Record concentrations and changes of solution.
  • Market-specific treatments, such as cold treatment for fruit fly or SO2 for grapes and litchis, must follow the approved protocol exactly.
  • Check that every treatment is accepted in the target market and within its residue limits.

Hygiene and traceability

  • Clean and sanitise dump tanks, brushes and conveyors on schedule.
  • Keep each lot traceable from bin to carton using block, PUC and packhouse codes.

A farm that does well in the orchard but delays cooling by a day can lose much of that quality. GAP means looking after the fruit at every step from planting to dispatch.

Key points

  • Plan site, cultivar, water and market registration before planting.
  • Use IPM and registered products, and respect pre-harvest intervals.
  • Determine the harvest window using maturity indices and sampling.
  • Handle fruit gently, keep it shaded and deliver it promptly.
  • Cool quickly and apply only approved post-harvest treatments.
